> 如是我闻。一时，佛在舍卫国祇树给孤独园，与大比丘众千二百五十人俱。尔时，世尊食时，著衣持钵，入舍卫大城乞食。饭食讫，收衣钵，洗足已，敷座而坐。

The Diamond Sutra opens with lunch.

Not with light, not with a rain of flowers, not with a bodhisattva descending. A teacher gets dressed, takes a bowl, walks into a city, accepts whatever is put in it, comes back, eats, puts the bowl away, washes his feet, and sits down. That is the whole of the first section. No doctrine is spoken in it.

Western readers usually treat this as scene-setting to be skipped. But the sutra is making an argument by arrangement: the teaching that later says *do not abide anywhere* begins by showing a man who has just put everything down.

## 如是我闻 is an audited signature, not a claim of authority

The first four characters are a record label: *thus have I heard*. 阿难, who recites the text at the first council, marks it as hearing rather than as invention. The formula does three things at once — it says this has a lineage, it says this can be checked, and it quietly says the "I" who heard is itself a conventional name.

That is worth pausing on. The sentence that opens the sutra already contains the structure the sutra will spend thirty-two sections unpacking: a transmission that is real in function and empty of a fixed owner. The book puts it bluntly: the first line has already planted the "即非" that comes later.

## 一时 is not a date

*At one time.* Every sutra says this and none of them say when. The convention marks the moment when a capacity and a teaching meet — not a point on a calendar. Time, in this grammar, is also a conventional designation, arising with conditions.

The effect is a specific kind of precision: the place is exact (a garden in a named city, bought with gold laid over the ground), the audience is counted (twelve hundred and fifty), the hour is named (the meal hour, before noon, per the rule), and the date is withheld.

## 次第乞 already performs what section three will argue

The monks beg in order, house to house, without choosing. They do not skip the poor house to reach the rich one, and they do not skip the rich house to make a display of poverty. No selection is made.

This matters because of what comes later: a long passage on the four signs — self, person, being, lifespan — and on the bodhisattva who liberates beings while holding no notion of beings liberated. Section one has already done it with the body. The argument in words arrives after the demonstration in practice. That is the sutra's teaching rhythm, and it is why the book insists this section cannot be skipped: *应无所住而生其心* without this would be a slogan with no floor under it.

## 洗足已，敷座而坐

Wash the feet; spread the seat; sit.

The feet are washed because they walked through dust. The seat is spread because the body needs a place. Then sitting: the day's business is finished, and none of it is carried into the sitting.

Most of us do the opposite. We finish a task and arrive at the next moment still wearing it — the conversation we just had, the number we just saw, the email we have not answered. The residue continues to run. The first section's last four characters are a description of a person in whom the residue has stopped.

That is the demonstration. The next section is the question.

## The test

Think of the last thing you finished today. Not the biggest thing — the last thing. Then sit down, as you are, and check: is any part of it still walking around in you?

If it is, you have located the subject of the whole sutra. It is not "emptiness" in general. It is this: the day ends and the mind does not.
